thirty for the weapons, and thirteen for the Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and [the seed-syllable] Tvarṇa. These are joined with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *hum*, and *phaṭ*, as well as *mṛda* and the others.
(5) Having a lion’s face and fierce fangs, possessing a radiance like fire, and accompanied by Śivā;
resembling black collyrium, endowed with three round, red eyes,
and carrying in her two right hands a trident and a *ḍamaru* drum.
Carrying in her two left hands a sprout from the edge of the remaining [garland]...
wearing black garments, with blood [on her], and possessing a mouth of flesh, she is devoted to the dull-witted.
Adorned with ornaments of pearls, covered with the limbs of serpents,
resounding with the sound of loud laughter, and endowed with black antelope skins.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with flowers from the limbs [of the body] and other offerings.
Alternatively, there should be five jars provided with threads and wrapped in cloth.
Having placed water-pots filled with scented water, containing kusha grass and golden lotuses,
each resting on a separate sacrificial mound, covered with lids and adorned with sprouts,
and their bodies smeared with sandalwood paste; and having also placed a water-jar.
O Śivāmbikā, having likewise worshipped the goddess who is joined with her cover within the *astra* [mantra],
and having worshipped *Prāgutthā* all around and also *Pratyaṅgirā*,
they should request permission for the *homa* and enter the fire-sanctuary.
Having praised the fire within its own ritual vessel as before,
he should invoke his respective deities together with their limbs and attendants, such as Airāvata and others.
They should offer libations according to the rule, either to the image or together with the preceptor;
they should perform the offering of water (*arghya*), the recitation of mantras, silent chanting (*japa*), hymns of praise, and so forth.
(6) They should remain properly composed, each stationed correctly in their respective directions.
The fuel of Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Śamī is thus prescribed.

To the left of the spreading Palāśa tree, there should be sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds, Dūrvā grass, and milk; the fuel-sticks should be made of Tarkāra wood and one finger-breadth in length.
And fifty or even one hundred vessels of sacrificial offerings—
each of them they should offer while remaining intent on meditation upon the deity.
The expiatory oblation, the full oblation, accompanied by the offering of betel;
the gift of protection, the obstruction, the respectful offering (*arghya*), the limb of dissolution, and the complete withdrawal.

Afterwards, one who has the mantra as their body should perform the inner and outer bali offerings, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and the petitioning of the deity for the sake of the rite; then, through the grace of the deity, at the conclusion, one should perform the bestowal of the sacred ash (bhasma) upon the performer and all others in due order. (4)
Having bathed [the preceptor] with water from the divine pitcher, one should worship the guru. Whether this [act] was performed in a temple or likewise with the contents of the pitchers,
whatever expiation is intended for that purpose, one should sprinkle that [person].
The *diśāhoma* (directional oblation), known as *svaṣṭha*, is declared to be the destroyer of all misfortunes;
the second *diśāhoma* is specifically described therein.
The worship of the weapons of Pratyāṅgirā has thus been described;
the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, boiled rice, sesame seeds, and parched rice.

The fire sacrifice (homa) is performed in the directions of Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Sadyojāta respectively; (3) from the ritual bathing onwards until the end of the homa, this same procedure applies in the four directions.
I shall now describe the *saṃhitā-homa*, which cuts away all defects,
performed upon auspicious ground within the sacrificial mandala of this fire.
One should perform [the rite] either in the midst of the sacrificial fire during festivals and so forth, or upon a consecrated altar (sthaṇḍila).
Śiva, together with his limbs and retinue, is designated as the "Saṃhitā" in the scripture.
When the preceptor has been honored by those mantras [beginning with] *ga-jā-dya*,

he [should perform the rite] with *palāśa* wood-sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and cooked rice, each offered one hundred times with the *Śiva-aṇu* (the Śiva-mantra). [He should likewise offer] ten times that number for the *Aṅgas* and a hundred times for the *Brahmaṇas*.
Then, with the Ghorāṇu mantra, perform the fivefold oblation... (omitted)... ||
Thus, having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should complete the rite according to the injunctions.
The *samhitā-homa* with the *oṃ* syllable (*nava*) should be performed; indeed, the *mūrti-homa* is prescribed [next].
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) either at the edge of the fire-altar or elsewhere...
And the Śivakumbha, along with the Vardhanī, should be placed in its center, to its right.
In the eight directions, one should place eight jars equipped with weapons such as the vajra,
along with threads, lids, cloths, and gold.
One should worship Gajodakodara with elephant-flowers, incense, and lamps;
and one should worship Śiva in the central pitcher and the Aghora-weapon in the water-pot (karaka).
Then, the Kuru king should worship Śiva, together with his [retinue], in the central jar during the rite of the King of the Nightless [Ardharātra].
Having offered [the mantra] "namas te astrāya kumbhāṇḍāya svāhā," and having offered the weapon-mantra to the form [of the deity] with "namaḥ mūrtyai astrāya," [one should proceed].
Yet he possessed a voice like that of a thundercloud, awakened by the brilliance of a thousand suns;

his cave-like mouth was illuminated by the tips of his blazing teeth, and his three eyes, long tongue, and flaming hair were as majestic as a sacrificial fire. (2) His locks of hair were as beautiful as a blazing sacrificial fuel.
Wearing the sacred thread (upavīta) across all [his limbs], he held a trident, a sword, a spear, and a mallet.
Four-armed and four-faced, with a shimmering crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
he dances with great speed, adorned with ornaments of serpents.

One should properly array weapons all around, from the thunderbolt (*vajra*) up to the trident (*śūla*), for the purpose of destroying those who are arrogant due to their pride in gods, *dānavas*, and *daityas*.
One should worship [the deities] in the five directions— east, north-east, and south-west— in due order; (5) then,
on a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) resembling a hand or a leaf, which is situated in front of that [altar],
(6) or even upon a consecrated earthen mound (*sthaṇḍila*), the preceptor should [install] the fire.
Having praised [the deity] and performed the five purificatory rites, one should then generate the visualization.
There, having invoked [the deity], one should worship Ghorāstra along with its limbs in the fire of Śiva;
[offering] sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, sesame, milk, white dūrvā grass, and the three types of oblations— namely,
cooked food or [rice] mixed with ashes— in exactly fifty of each.
One should offer oblations individually with these [mantras] into the Śiva-fire using the Aghora-weapon mantra.
One should satisfy [the deities] with the limbs and weapons associated with the exposition of karma;
then, having offered the final oblation and completed the rite of atonement.
Again, having given those full offerings of betel, and having praised and prostrated,
the preceptor should perform the protection of the fire-oblation (*homarakṣā*) while [offering] the *argha* and [granting] the desired boon.
Having sprinkled water for the sake of the sacrificer, he should offer the *arghya* with his face turned away;
having performed the worship of the limbs of dissolution at the end, he should recite the *vyāhṛti* mantras over Śiva.
He should maintain the sacred fire in that very place until the ritual is completed.
Or he should perform the rite of oblation daily upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).

Having offered the inner and outer oblations and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one whose body is composed of the Aṇu-mantra should go to the pitcher and other implements, which are to be known as the objects of the ritual action, O Goddess who embodies the weapon-mantra.
Then, one should bathe the Supreme Lord with water from that jar,
and worship Him with perfumes, flowers, unguents, and so forth, at the conclusion of the food offering.

Having prayed and recited [the mantras], the ashes produced from the grace of the deity obtained [through that] should be given to the sacrificer after being heated for the protection of the oblation.
In this case as well, one should perform the mantra-recitation for half a year according to the ritual of pacification (śānti);
the "Mūrtihoma" and the "Savākhyahoma" are prescribed for the purpose of expiation.
Another specific feature of the *mūrti-homa* is stated therein:
one should worship the *kumbha*, the *astra*, and the *vardhanī*, as well as Śiva and Ambikā within the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*).
One should perform the fire oblation (homa) in the eight external pots,
starting from the southeast, using the mantras of the eight deities beginning with Karva and Śarva.
(…) on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) as prescribed for the *naiṛtikārya* rite, in eight fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), or in a single one provided with an eightfold altar (*vedikā*);
[he should offer] one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sesame seeds (*tila*), milk, and barley, (2) or fifty in number,
or even half of that, separately for each.
Palāśa, udumbara, aśvattha, and so forth, in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The *śamyā*, *khā*, *mārga*, *śrī*, *puṣpa*, and *va* [are] declared as the *samithas*;
[they are formed] with [the syllables] excluding *indra* (*i*), accompanied by *pāva* and *kuṇḍa*.
On a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) facing east, measuring five cubits or as desired,
one should perform the ritual of fire-oblation (*homatantra*) with the serpent-mantras (*sarpamantra*).
In the eastern [direction],
having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with the hymn from the *Īśakuṇḍelāguru-saṃhitā*, one should then cause Śiva to bathe with the eight [substances].
Having worshipped with *gajapuṣpa* and other offerings, one should pray for the attainment of one's desired goal.
Thus, according to the distinctions such as "excellent" (*śreṣṭha*) and so forth, [the practice] removes the afflictions caused by sleepiness, lassitude, and the nature of [worldly] attachment.
Beyond the fruit of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), in the three worlds of dwellings and merchandise,
merely by the water of the crest-ornament (*cūlikodaka*), it shall become a cause for the pleasure of Śiva.
A single jar is superior to thousands of prasthas of water;
a prastha of ghee is superior to thousands of jars of that [water].
A prastha of curd is superior to thousands of prasthas of milk.
A single *prastha* of ghee is superior to a thousand *prasthas* of curd;
a single *prastha* of honey is superior to a thousand *prasthas* of ghee;
and *pañcagavya* is distinguished as superior to a thousand *prasthas* of honey. (4–5)
Beyond the five thousand [units] of the five products of the cow comes the five nectars;
and superior even to the five nectars, the essence of fruit is distinguished as the most excellent.
The essence of the fruit is superior, and its essence is especially superior;
they know that one *prastha* of fragrant water is to be understood as being even more excellent than the essence of sugarcane.
They know that from thousands of *iṣṭhu* measures on its slopes comes a thousandfold stream;
by thousands of streams of a thousandfold [measure], the *khaṭga* vessel is distinguished.
A single conch shell is superior to a thousand swords and vessels;
among thousands of such conch shells, they know the one that spirals to the right to be the most distinguished.
There is nothing superior to bathing with a right-turning conch shell.
